newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia seeks NATO compromise at partnership talks.
newsitem.headline: Russia seeks NATO compromise at partnership talks.

text.p: Russia, taking a firm line before a visit to Moscow by NATO Secretary General Javier Solana, accused the alliance on Monday of skimping on compromise in efforts to forge a partnership between the former Cold War foes.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said President Boris Yeltsin and Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, in last- minute strategy talks, had repeated a desire to reach agreement mapping out a peaceful relationship with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
But Yastrzhembsky, adopting a tactic used by the Kremlin on the eve of previous rounds of negotiations, said Moscow would not sign any agreement that did not reflect its interests.
"Such an agreement must be reached on an equal basis, but not at all costs," Yastrzhembsky told Interfax news agency.
Some NATO members "are not showing enough desire to seek a compromise," said Yastrzhembsky, who this month took on extra responsibilities for coordinating foreign policy in the Kremlin.

Moscow opposes NATO's plans to take in members from the former Soviet bloc, but Primakov said last week in Paris that Yeltsin hoped to sign an agreement mapping out post-Cold War relations with the alliance on May 27.
That would be weeks before a NATO summit in Madrid on July 6, at which Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are expected to receive membership invitations.

Yastrzhembsky, echoing comments by NATO diplomats, said there had been progress in work on preparing documents for signing and reiterated Moscow's overall readiness to complete a substantial "binding" agreement.

But, although Yeltsin seemed reconciled to the idea of NATO's expansion at a summit in Helsinki last month with U.S. President Bill Clinton, some Western diplomats say Moscow has toughened its negotiating stance since then and adopted a hard line.
Yeltsin has to play to the opposition communists and nationalists in Russia who are ready to pounce on any sign that he is not defending Russia's interests.
Moscow wants restrictions on the movement of NATO troops and equipment, including nuclear weapons, into new member states.
It also wants a commitment from the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation that it will not build or upgrade facilities to take such weapons at a later date, Western diplomats say.

Comments by Russian officials suggest Moscow may not be confident of reaching an agreement by May 27, despite Primakov's remarks in Paris. Talks are far from complete, a foreign ministry source told Interfax.
"We are realists and understand that we are still a long way from that (a final agreement)," the source said.
A NATO source added: "Time frameworks are not the most important thing."
The Kremlin gave no details of Yeltsin's discussions on NATO with Primakov, but they were sure to have covered Solana's visit and Yeltsin's plans to visit NATO member Germany this week.

Yeltsin praised Primakov for mediating a breakthrough at talks between Moldova and its breakaway Dnestr region last week which paves the way for them to normalise relations after a bloody conflict in 1992.

He did not mention his work in negotiations with NATO or his role in the preparation of a union treaty with Belarus. The accord was criticised by liberals and the Russian media and was watered down by the Kremlin at the last minute.
